references.text: Human wickedness—'the thoughts and devices of the human heart were evil all day long'—supports Jesus' words that people are 'evil' (πονηροί) by nature.
Solomon's prayer reflects that people are inclined to evil, which aligns with Jesus' statement that even though people are evil, they can still give good gifts.

The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same argument from the lesser to the greater: If evil people give good gifts to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give good gifts to those who ask him. In Matthew, 'good gifts' is used, while Luke specifically mentions the Holy Spirit.
Joel's prophecy that God will pour out his Spirit on all people—a promise of the gift of the Holy Spirit which Jesus here links to prayer.
God's promise through Isaiah to pour out his Spirit upon the offspring of Israel, which corresponds with the promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.
God's promise to put his Spirit within his people—an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit.
Jesus promises that the Father will give another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, to the disciples—an elaboration on the promise of the Holy Spirit as a gift from the Father.
Jesus says it is for the disciples' benefit that he goes away, for then he will send the Advocate—the Holy Spirit—to them.
Jesus commands the disciples to wait for the Father's promise—the baptism in the Holy Spirit—which is a fulfillment of the promise in Luke 11:13 that the Father gives the Spirit.
Pentecost fulfills the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask, as the disciples who had prayed and waited were filled with the Spirit.
Peter urges the people to repent and be baptized with the promise of the gift of the Holy Spirit—a confirmation that God gives the Spirit to those who seek him.
Paul writes that believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit when they came to faith—a confirmation that the Father gives the Spirit as a gift.
Jesus told the parable of the widow and the judge to show that disciples should always pray and not lose heart—emphasizing perseverance in prayer, just as the context in Luke 11 does.
The immediate context with the parable of the friend who knocks at midnight, teaching boldness and perseverance in prayer, and the promise that whoever asks will receive.

James writes that 'every good gift and every perfect gift' comes from above, from the Father of lights—this agrees with Jesus' words that the Father in heaven gives good gifts, especially the Holy Spirit.

Paul describes how believers have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry out 'Abba, Father!' – The Holy Spirit given by the Father confirms the close relationship between God and his children, as Luke 11:13 presupposes.
